issues.text: Whether the applicant complied with the requirement to exhaust domestic remedies before applying to the Court

anchor.surface_text: requirement to exhaust domestic remedies is normally assessed with reference to the date on which the application was lodged with the Court. However, the Court’s well-established case-law shows that it allows the last stage of a particular remedy to be reached after the application has been lodged but before its admissibility has been determined (see Karoussiotis v. Portugal, no. 23205/08, § 57, ECHR 2011 (extracts); Mehmet Hasan Altan, cited above, § 107; Şahin Alpay v. Turkey, no. 16538/17, § 86, 20 March 2018; Molla Sali v. Greece [GC], no. 20452/14, §§ 90-91, 19 December 2018; and A.M. v. France, no. 12148/18, § 66, 29 April 2019). The applicant in the present case lodged her application with the Court on 7 September 2017. The individual application which she had lodged with the Constitutional Court on 29 May 2017 was declared inadmissible on 18 July 2018, before the Court’s decision on admissibility.

issues.text: Whether the applicant raised her complaints under Article 5 § 3 of the Convention before the Constitutional Court

anchor.surface_text: applicant explicitly relied on Article 5 § 3 of the Convention before that court. She clearly complained about the lack of reasoning in the decisions concerning her detention (pages 8 and 15 of the application form) and about the failure to apply an alternative measure to pre-trial detention (page 16 of the same form). The Court notes that, in its decision, the Constitutional Court examined the reasoning provided by the Diyarbakır 3rd Magistrate’s Court in the detention order. The higher court held that the magistrate’s findings regarding the proportionality of the detention measure and the inadequacy of alternative measures had neither been arbitrary nor unfounded (see paragraph 44 above).

arguments.claim: The applicant submitted that the prosecuting authorities and the domestic courts had failed to provide reasonable evidence that she had committed the criminal offences of which she was suspected.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant submitted that the prosecuting authorities and the domestic courts had failed to provide reasonable evidence that she had committed the criminal offences of which she was suspected. She asserted that the decisions taken against her had been based solely on her political activities during her tenure as a member of parliament. The applicant maintained that press statements, meetings and demonstrations in which she had participated in her capacity as a politician had been unjustly treated as grounds for suspicion. She alleged that, like many other members of the HDP, she had been detained as part of a broader strategy by the public authorities to silence political opposition.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found no reasonable suspicion based on the evidence and considered the detention unjustified.

arguments.claim: The applicant asserted that the primary reason for her pre-trial detention had been her role as co-chair of the Democratic Society Congress, which was a lawful organisation aimed at peaceful solutions.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant asserted that the primary reason for her pre-trial detention had been her role as co-chair of the Democratic Society Congress. She argued that the DTK had been established to seek peaceful solutions to societal issues and had never supported violence or any illegal armed organisation. She maintained that the DTK could not be criminalised merely because its objective of achieving peace aligned with the aims of an illegal armed organisation.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found no indication that the DTK was regarded as unlawful during the applicant's tenure and no evidence linking it to criminal activity.

arguments.claim: The applicant argued that the decisions ordering her detention were formulaic, lacked individualised assessment, and failed to consider less restrictive alternatives.

anchor.surface_text: Furthermore, she argued that the decisions ordering both her initial and continued pre-trial detention had been based on formulaic reasoning and lacked any individualised assessment of her personal circumstances or the specific facts of the case. She maintained that the judicial authorities had failed to engage with the arguments she had raised in favour of her release and had not demonstrated why less restrictive alternatives, such as judicial supervision, would have been inadequate in her case.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found no reasonable suspicion and thus did not need to assess the sufficiency of reasoning or alternatives.

arguments.claim: The Government argued that the applicant had been placed in detention on the basis of concrete evidence for the offence of establishing or leading an illegal armed organisation.

anchor.surface_text: The Government argued that the applicant had been placed in detention on the basis of concrete evidence for the offence of establishing or leading an illegal armed organisation. They stated that, at the time of her pre‑trial detention, there had been sufficient evidence to convince an objective observer that she had served as co-chair of the DTK and had acted in accordance with the orders of PKK executives.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the evidence insufficient to establish reasonable suspicion.

arguments.claim: The Government asserted that the applicant had participated in demonstrations, meetings, press statements and funerals of PKK members organised by the DTK and had sought to engage in self-criticism in line with the policies of the illegal armed organisation.

anchor.surface_text: They alleged that she had participated in demonstrations, meetings, press statements and funerals of PKK members organised by the DTK; that she had sought to engage in self-criticism in line with the policies of the illegal armed organisation; that she had openly criticised the DTK structure; and that she had given interviews on Roj TV, a channel controlled by the PKK.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found no concrete evidence linking these activities to criminal offence.

arguments.claim: The Government submitted three Court of Cassation decisions supporting the link between DTK and PKK/KCK illegal armed organisation.

anchor.surface_text: The Government asserted that, in various decisions, national judicial authorities had stressed the organic link between the DTK and the PKK/KCK organisation. To support this assertion, the Government submitted three decisions delivered by the Court of Cassation.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court noted these decisions did not assess DTK's nature or involve its leaders and thus were insufficient evidence.

arguments.claim: The Government argued that the applicant's role as co-chair of the DTK on orders of PKK/KCK leaders and her activities aligned with its aims established reasonable suspicion.

anchor.surface_text: The Government further noted that, during both the investigation and the proceedings, the applicant had admitted to serving as co-chair of the DTK. They submitted that the fact that the applicant had assumed the role of co‑chair of the DTK on the orders of the leaders of the PKK/KCK and that her activities had aligned with its aims had been sufficient to establish reasonable suspicion that she had committed the offence of forming or leading a terrorist organisation.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found no concrete evidence to support this claim and rejected it.

arguments.claim: The Government argued that the applicant had participated in unlawful demonstrations and meetings, made statements inciting violence and armed rebellion, and sought to disrupt Türkiye’s territorial integrity.

anchor.surface_text: The Government further argued that the applicant had participated in several unlawful demonstrations and meetings, during which she had made statements inciting violence and armed rebellion and had sought to disrupt Türkiye’s territorial integrity by advocating for autonomy in certain regions of the country.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found no evidence linking statements to violent events and considered them political opinions.

arguments.claim: The Government maintained that the applicant’s detention was justified given the complexity, nature of offence, severity of penalty, and risk of absconding or tampering with evidence.

anchor.surface_text: The Government submitted that the detention measure had been in compliance with the law and that the evidence referred to by the domestic courts had been sufficient to demonstrate that the applicant had committed the offence attributed to her, namely that of forming or leading a terrorist organisation.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found no reasonable suspicion and thus detention was not justified.

arguments.claim: The Government argued that the interference with the applicant’s freedom of expression was lawful, necessary for national security, public safety, and prevention of disorder or crime.

anchor.surface_text: In any event, any interference by the authorities had been in accordance with the law and necessary in the interests of national security, public safety, and for the prevention of disorder or crime.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the interference was not justified as the statements were political expression, not incitement.

arguments.claim: The applicant submitted that her pre-trial detention violated Article 10 because her speeches contained no incitement to violence or terrorist propaganda and were political expression.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant submitted that her pre-trial detention had been in breach of Article 10 because her speeches had not contained any elements of incitement to violence or terrorist propaganda. She claimed that she had made speeches in her capacity as co-chair of DTK, a lawful organisation, and as a politician.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court accepted that the statements were political opinions and protected under Article 10.

arguments.claim: The Government invited the Court to declare the Article 10 complaint inadmissible as incompatible ratione materiae under Article 17, alleging the applicant produced terrorist propaganda and incited violence.

anchor.surface_text: The Government invited the Court to declare the complaint under Article 10 inadmissible as being incompatible ratione materiae with the provisions of the Convention, arguing that the applicant’s acts fell within the scope of Article 17 of the Convention in that, by her speeches and statements, she, as the co-chair of the DTK, had (i) produced propaganda for a terrorist organisation and (ii) incited people to violence.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found no evidence that the applicant intended to incite violence or hatred and dismissed the objection.

arguments.claim: The Court found that the applicant’s initial and continued detention on account of her statements amounted to an interference with her freedom of expression.

anchor.surface_text: In the light of the foregoing, the Court considers that the applicant’s initial and continued detention on account of her statements amounted to an interference with the exercise of her freedom of expression.
